slides.title: Why the margin fell
Wages are not the main cause: gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment explain 79% of the margin decline since FY2023

claims.claim: 79% of the fall comes from gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment
evidence: Chart, operating margin % of sales, FY2023 to FY2025: FY2023 margin 0.033732; Gross margin 0.01019; Store labor 0.002996; Occupancy and energy 0.001985; E-commerce fulfillment 0.008381; Other SG&A 1e-06; FY2025 margin 0.01018

claims.claim: Gross margin: the largest step, driven by deeper promotions and higher shrink
E-commerce fulfillment: cost grew 3.5 times as fast-growing home delivery outran its fees
Store labor: 13% of the fall; the hours cut to offset wages fed part of the shrink rise
Other SG&A: flat as a share of sales, so no lever here

slides.title: Productivity has already absorbed most of the wage rise, with 6% fewer hours per sale against a 9.4% higher hourly wage

claims.claim: The pressure management points to: 9.4% average hourly wage incl. benefits
evidence: $16.80 an hour in FY2023, $18.38 in FY2025
Driven by the state minimum wage and a tight labor market
A further 4% minimum-wage rise is due in 2027

claims.claim: Productivity offset most of the wage rise: −5.98% labor hours per $1,000 of sales
evidence: 7.02 hours in FY2023, 6.60 in FY2025
Hours grew more slowly than sales
Shrink rose over the same years, from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales

claims.claim: A small part of the margin fall: 0.3 pp store labor as a share of sales
evidence: 11.8% of sales in FY2023, 12.1% in FY2025
Against a fall of 2.35 percentage points in operating margin

claims.claim: Cutting hours targets the smallest of the causes

slides.title: The gross-margin fall comes entirely from deeper promotions and higher shrink, both within Harlow's control

claims.claim: $18.04M of gross profit a year lost to the two drifts, at FY2025 sales
evidence: Chart, gross margin % of sales: FY2023 gross margin 0.260423; Promotional mix 0.007; Private-label mix 0.0018; Shrink 0.005; FY2025 gross margin 0.250233

claims.claim: Promotional mix: promotions rose from 24% to 29% of sales, each sale earning 14 percentage points less margin
Vendor funding: vendors now cover 46% of markdowns, down from 55%, so each event costs Harlow more
Shrink: up from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales as hours per sale fell
Private label: share rose from 17.0% to 18.5% at 12 percentage points more margin, too slowly to offset
evidence: Mix effects use the margin gaps in the briefing pack (promotions −14 pp, private label +12 pp, both unchanged); the three drivers explain the full change

slides.title: What promotions and e-commerce really earn
Promotions are not paying back: 38% of FY2025 events lost money, and more shoppers now see Harlow as expensive

claims.claim: Promotional share of sales rose 5 percentage points in two years
evidence: +5 pp
Promotional share: FY2023 0.24; FY2024 0.262; FY2025 0.29

claims.claim: Yet more shoppers call Harlow more expensive than other options
evidence: +8 pp
More expensive: FY2023 0.33; FY2025 0.41
Customer survey, n = 3,100

claims.claim: And many events lose money outright: 38% of events lost money after counting the extra units sold
evidence: FY2025 promotional events, post-event review

claims.claim: Vendor funding fell to 46% of markdowns from 55%
The category team's case (1.8% comparable growth in the deepest-promoting stores, against 0.2%) measures sales, not profit
evidence: the category team's comparison does not control for store location or the ValuMart openings

claims.claim: Stores near ValuMart still fell 4.2% in comparable sales

slides.title: Counted in full, e-commerce lost about $10M in FY2025, and home delivery causes 91% of the loss

claims.claim: e-commerce lost about $10M in FY2025
evidence: Chart, $ millions: Contribution on new sales 7.66656; Picking 9.8494; Third-party delivery 10.6533; Delivery fees 2.39314; E-commerce result -10.443
Contribution on new sales = $127.8M e-commerce sales × 30% new to Harlow (survey of 2,300 customers, stated intent) × 20 cents (finance estimate)
Fulfillment lines add up to the $18.1M in the income statement

claims.claim: 91% of the loss comes from home-delivered orders
evidence: Per order: a home delivery loses about $12.34; a click-and-collect order about $1.64

claims.claim: The team's 6.1% margin: leaves out third-party delivery and counts every online sale as new to Harlow
Only 30% is new: shoppers say 70% of what they buy online they would otherwise buy in a Harlow store

slides.title: Why the labor cut falls short
Hours cuts would raise shrink: the leanest-staffed stores already lose 3.1% of sales to it, against 2.3% in the best-staffed

claims.claim: Hours protect against shrink up to the Q3 level, and little beyond it
evidence: Shrink, % of sales, FY2025: Q1, fewest hours 0.031; Q2 0.027; Q3 0.024; Q4, most hours 0.023; Chain average 0.026

claims.claim: Q1, fewest hours: managers say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days
What leaks: fresh waste and receiving errors make up 65% of shrink, the tasks that need staff time
Q4, most hours: only 0.1 percentage points less shrink than Q3, so these stores can give up hours
Gain a year if Q1 and Q2 stores reach the Q3 rate: $3.8M
evidence: (0.7 + 0.3) pp ÷ 4 quartiles × $1,503M sales
Quartiles assumed to carry equal sales; their average matches the chain's 2.6%

slides.title: Even counting only staff-sensitive shrink, management's hours cut would net about $8M a year, not $14.5M

claims.claim: Net saving from 8% fewer scheduled store hours: $14.5M − $6.5M = $8M
evidence: $14.5M gross saving a year, management's estimate for 8% fewer hours
$6.5M added shrink: waste and receiving errors, 65% of shrink, rise with fewer hours as in FY2023–25
$8M net saving a year, before any lost sales

claims.claim: The net figure is likely an upper bound
evidence: Shrink rose 0.5 percentage points as hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6% in FY2023–25; only its staff-sensitive 65% is assumed to respond to a further 8% cut
If theft responds to thinner staffing too, the net saving falls to about $4.5M a year
Lost sales from longer checkout waits and stock-outs are not counted, while ValuMart keeps opening nearby
The 2027 minimum-wage rise of 4% adds about $7.3M a year to the labor bill under either plan

claims.claim: The draft also freezes e-commerce at a loss and leaves promotions and shrink untouched

fee test on FY2025 orders, less lost sales

normalized.recommendation: Fix promotions, shrink and home delivery rather than cut labor: approve the plan (five moves: delivery fees, promotions, store hours and shrink, private label, six store exits) and replace the across-the-board 8% hours cut. Delivery fees, promotion cuts and shrink fixes go first (wave 1); the CFO should open covenant talks with the lender now. Decision today: approve wave 1 and replace the across-the-board hours cut.

alternatives_considered.option: Management draft: 8% fewer store hours, e-commerce frozen
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: would net about $8M, not $14.5M, because shrink rises where hours are thin; leaves FY2028 margin near 1.3% (1.75% if shrink does not respond) vs about 2.3% for the recommended plan; freezes e-commerce at a loss and leaves promotions and shrink untouched. Draft is safer for the covenant on paper (about $23.0M; $19.4M if all of the shrink rise came from staffing), at a cost in shrink and service.

alternatives_considered.option: Exit the three stores with longer leases
alternatives_considered.treatment: Deferred: $2.2M a year, $7.5M one-time exit cost, payback about 3.4 years, needs a board vote; decide in FY2028, after wave 1 shows whether these stores recover.

alternatives_considered.option: Exit the six stores whose leases end by 2027
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen: $4.4M a year, no exit cost and no board vote needed; start here.

alternatives_considered.option: Freeze/drop home delivery vs keep it with the tested fee
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended plan keeps home delivery with the tested fee (owners' condition met: home delivery stays on offer); the draft freezes it at today's size, still losing money.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Quartiles assumed to carry equal sales; their average matches the chain's 2.6%
The shrink response is inferred from FY2023–25, not measured store by store
The net figure (labor cut $8M) is likely an upper bound; if theft responds to thinner staffing too, the net saving falls to about $4.5M a year
Lost sales from longer checkout waits and stock-outs are not counted, while ValuMart keeps opening nearby
A 10-week test in 4 stores; results assumed to hold chain-wide
Store-level P&L is needed to confirm the even split; four-wall EBITDA excludes head-office costs, which do not fall away
Run-rates at FY2025 sales and volumes; small overlaps not netted
Plan starts from FY2025 with no further drift and no cost inflation beyond the 4% wage rise; occupancy alone rose $3.9M a year in FY2023–25
3.0% needs nearly everything to go right; low case 1.97% if promotions return only to FY2024 share of 26.2%
Covenant: the decline must stop, and the test year needs confirming with the lender; if the FY2025 fall of $18.1M repeated, wave 1 would need more than its full-year value
The briefing pack treats FY2026 as the first plan year; the CFO should confirm with the lender how much of it remains
30% new-to-Harlow e-commerce share is from a survey of 2,300 customers, stated intent; 20 cents contribution is a finance estimate
The category team's comparison does not control for store location or the ValuMart openings
Recommended plan's main risk: traffic loss near ValuMart as promotions fall
